Refined sub-Gaussian framework capturing token distribution anisotropy through interpretable coupling coefficients (attention horizon H and attention-token coupling Ψ)
Comprehensive multi-level analysis: pointwise convergence, uniform convergence on balls, and moment convergence with explicit dependence on attention geometry and data properties
Novel hardmax asymptotics (Proposition 5.5) revealing symmetry-driven cancellation with exact rates σ/√ln n for Gaussian case

Convincing experimental validation on synthetic Gaussian data showing tight agreement with theory; real data experiments (BigBird on Wikipedia) demonstrating sub-parametric convergence rates β < 1/2 in practice across multiple languages

Limited scope to single attention layer with fixed parameters; no analysis of deep stacking, residual connections, or layer-wise error propagation despite practical relevance

Hardmax analysis (Proposition 5.5) restricted to 1D Gaussian case; claimed extensions to non-Gaussian real embeddings justified by intuition ('skewness, kurtosis') rather than rigorous analysis

Limited experimental scope: only BigBird-RoBERTa-base tested (small model); no modern LLMs; measures only mean/covariance convergence, not downstream task performance or actual utility of extended context
Assumes i.i.d. tokens despite acknowledgment that natural text violates this; robustness not rigorously established

strengths: Novel problem formulation: Token sample complexity provides a fresh and timely perspective for understanding attention in long-context Transformers, clearly distinguished from classical PAC complexity

Rigorous mathematical analysis: Handles non-trivial technical challenges including autocorrelation in self-attention, dimension reduction for vector-valued processes, and explicit quantitative bounds from empirical process theory

Meaningful theoretical insights: Discovers sub-parametric convergence rates (n^{-β} with β < 1/2) contradicting naive expectations, characterizes dependence on data geometry through interpretable coupling coefficients, and provides exact asymptotics for hardmax regime
Theory-practice alignment: Experiments on both synthetic Gaussian and real BERT data validate theoretical predictions, demonstrating observed rates match across multiple layers and datasets
Comprehensive treatment: Provides multiple perspectives (pointwise, uniform, moment-level), covers multiple distributional regimes, and includes both theoretical analysis and empirical validation

Sound technical execution: Proofs correctly apply empirical process theory with appropriate techniques (Dudley's entropy integral, sub-Gaussian concentration, extreme value theory), with detailed appendix documentation
weaknesses: Limited tightness of bounds: Theorem 4.2's constant grows exponentially in radius R (e^{8R²||Σ^{1/2}A||²₂}), becoming uninformative for large R; bounds in Theorem 5.3 acknowledged as not sharp in full generality, limiting quantitative practical utility

Gap between theory and practice: Assumes i.i.d. tokens from fixed distribution while real text has strong dependencies; assumes fixed pre-trained models while practical applications involve fine-tuning; sub-Gaussian assumption may not hold universally

Modest practical impact: Bounds involve problem-dependent constants (||Σ||₂, ||A||₂) difficult to estimate; results largely confirmatory rather than prescriptive; no actionable insights for model design or practitioners beyond 'longer contexts help'

Incomplete technical analysis: Hardmax analysis limited to 1D Gaussian with extension to higher dimensions unclear; intuition for exponent β = 1/(2(1+32Ψ)) could be better developed; relationship between single-query horizon H and distribution-dependent moments unclear

Experimental limitations: Real data uses relatively small subsample sizes (n ∈ [1000, 3000]); only BigBird/RoBERTa tested; no comparison of theoretical bounds to actual observed errors; no analysis on structurally diverse or adversarial token distributions

Limited novelty relative to concurrent work: Boursier & Boyer (2025) establishes similar O(1/n^β) rates with overlapping analysis; positioning as building on recent foundational measure-field Transformer work (Geshkovski et al. 2024-2025) suggests somewhat incremental contribution

Missing practical extensions: No analysis of causal attention (standard in practice), handling of intermediate layer transformations, or guidance for when practitioners should worry about token sample complexity

strengths: Novel problem formulation: Token sample complexity as n increases at fixed parameters is timely and well-motivated given long-context LLM trends
Rigorous mathematical framework: Proper use of measure theory, empirical processes, and extreme value theory with careful handling of technical challenges (non-Lipschitz softmax, dependent Q/K/V)
Attention horizon as unifying concept: Identification of H = ||Σ^(1/2)AΣ^(1/2)||₂ governing convergence, with clear geometric interpretation
Multiple analytical perspectives: Pointwise convergence (Theorem 4.2), moment convergence (Theorem 5.3), and hardmax limit provide complementary insights
Strong experimental validation: Theory-practice agreement on Gaussian data, systematic evaluation across BigBird/BERT layers/languages, convincing downstream task experiments
Practical insights: Demonstration that 25% of keys recover most accuracy; downstream slowdown matches theoretical predictions
Comprehensive treatment: Full proofs in appendix, multiple extensions (covariance, deep composition, compactly supported), honest discussion of limitations
weaknesses: Theorem 4.2 exponential dependence: e^(8R²||Σ^(1/2)A||²₂) bound is uninformative for realistic radii R; acknowledged issue but not resolved in main result
Sub-parametric rates arbitrarily slow: Exponent β = 1/(2(1+32H²)) approaches 0 for large H; practical convergence becomes impractical in high-horizon regimes
Theory-practice gap: Analysis assumes fixed parameters, but practical transformers train end-to-end; relationship between training-time and inference-time token behavior unexplored
i.i.d. assumption restrictive: Real token sequences have dependencies; theoretical guarantees only for i.i.d. sampling despite empirical evidence for window-based sampling
Hardmax analysis limited: Proposition 5.5 restricted to 1D Gaussian; cancellation phenomenon is Gaussian-specific; condition ||Aσ||₂ ≫ 1 may not hold in practice
Complicated constants limit applicability: Polynomial P in Theorem 5.3, constant q in Theorem 4.2 lack explicit forms; practitioners cannot easily apply bounds
Limited practical guidance: Paper does not explain how to use convergence rates to improve models or allocate computational resources
Incomplete sparse attention analysis: Limited comparison to existing methods (Linformer, Performer); window-based sampling only briefly explored

strengths: Introduces novel and timely concept of token sample complexity relevant to long-context LLMs
Comprehensive three-regime theoretical analysis: uniform convergence, moment convergence, and hardmax limit
Identifies attention horizon H as an interpretable quantity governing convergence rates
Technical sophistication in applying empirical process theory with appropriate handling of non-Lipschitz kernels
Attempts to connect theory to downstream performance (Figure 2)
weaknesses: Critical theory-practice gap: Theorem 4.2 has impractical exponential dependence on R; Theorem 5.3 gives n^{-β} rates with β≈0.003 for H=1, making convergence unrealistically slow for practical guidance

Restrictive and incompletely justified assumptions: i.i.d. tokens (contradicts sequential dependencies in text), sub-Gaussian embeddings (not validated), fixed limit distribution ν (questionable relevance)
Insufficient motivation for problem relevance: paper studies infinite-token limit but doesn't explain why this matters for realistic finite, dependent sequences

Impractical bound constants: Theorem 4.2 has complex unanalyzed constants q(Σ,A,V,R,d,δ); no explicit characterization of bounds for realistic scenarios
Missing lower bounds proving tightness; no sensitivity analysis for assumption violations; Proposition 5.5 restricted to 1D Gaussian with symmetry requirements not met by real embeddings

Rigorous theoretical analysis across multiple regimes (uniform convergence Theorem 4.2, moment convergence Theorem 5.3, hardmax limit Proposition 5.5) using sophisticated empirical process theory
Identification of attention horizon H = ||Σ^{1/2}AΣ^{1/2}||₂ as the key quantity governing convergence rates, with clear geometric interpretation

Strong empirical validation: synthetic results precisely match theory (Figure 3); real data experiments across BigBird/BERT, multiple layers, languages, and datasets show predicted horizon-dependent slowdown
Careful technical handling of challenging aspects: non-uniformly Lipschitz softmax, dependence between Q/K/V (improvement over concurrent work), ratio convergence
Comprehensive experiments including end-to-end downstream task validation and structured (windowed) sampling beyond i.i.d.
Clear presentation of complex topic with good motivation, logical progression, and practical insights (e.g., 25% of keys recovers most accuracy)
weaknesses: Constants in bounds are not tight: Theorem 4.2 has c(R) ∝ exp(8R²||Σ^{1/2}A||₂²) growing exponentially, and Theorem 5.3 contains unexplained factor of 32 in β = 1/(2(1+32H²)); gap between worst-case theory and smoother empirical convergence

Strong assumptions with theory-practice gaps: (1) i.i.d. token sampling contradicts sequential nature of text (Appendix A discussion is informal), (2) fixed distribution ν ignores adaptive attention, (3) fixed model parameters don't capture training dynamics
Sub-Gaussian assumption not empirically validated on real embeddings; Appendix C.9 shows heavy-tailed failure case but no analysis of when/where this occurs in practice
